extracted.intended_audience: improvisers, improv teachers, students, and theatre practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for performing, producing and teaching improvisation (short- and long-form), covering artistic aims, formats that manage risk, storytelling, innovation, and classroom/workshop practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvisation is more than ad‑libbing
rubrics_metrics.description: Improvisation is not simply ad‑libbing or extemporizing; it can create comedy or drama, and should aim to be artful spontaneous creation rather than casual gagging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid treating improv as mere free-form jokework. Recognize it can produce genuine theatrical work; aim for craft and intentionality rather than relying on the label 'it's just improv' as a free pass.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short form tends toward comedy; long form permits emotional depth
rubrics_metrics.description: Short form sketches are usually comedic and it's difficult for an audience to take a sequence of short tragic scenes; in contrast, improvised stories of forty minutes to an hour allow the audience to invest in characters and accept genuine emotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose format according to desired tone: use short form for rapid comedy and long form when you want emotional authenticity and character development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Storytelling and narrative framework are essential
rubrics_metrics.description: If no emphasis at all is placed on storytelling, improvisation can quickly dissolve into slurry that provides nothing memorable for the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritise plot, character and coherence where appropriate; without narrative structure, performers may over-rely on being funny every moment and produce forgettable work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage the 'two stories' (scene story vs performers' struggle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Improvisers always tell two stories: the story within their scenes/games and the meta-story of their struggle for glory; a good show identifies which of the two is more interesting at any moment and emphasizes that.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether the audience should focus on the fictional scene or on performers taking risks/competing; use formats and staging to balance these narratives deliberately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use structural mechanisms to handle failure and encourage risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Formats with built‑in mechanisms (e.g., Theatresports, Micetro Impro, Gorilla Theatre) remind the audience of improvised nature and provide 'outs' or scoring/elimination that allow players to take daring choices without killing the show.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt or design formats that normalize variability of hit-rate and make failure an acceptable, even entertaining, part of the performance; this increases the frequency of genuine successes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embrace risk/high‑wire aspect as part of the appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: The best improvisers make the audience aware of the risk they are taking; showing the possibility of failure (the high-wire act) is an essential and thrilling part of improv.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protect and foreground the sense of danger or unpredictability in performance where appropriate; do not eliminate risk to pursue polished but sterile results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commitment to invented reality—'if we commit, the audience will believe'
rubrics_metrics.description: Because improv is inexpensive and compact, whatever performers tell the audience is in that space the audience will believe if the performers commit, e.g., miming a device or embodying a character convincingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Never treat low production requirements as an excuse for laziness; strong commitment to physical and emotional choices sells scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid treating improvisation casually despite low commercial cost
rubrics_metrics.description: The fact that improv costs little can lead to it being treated as an art form of little value; this casual attitude undermines quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hold improvisation to standards of craft and seriousness even if budgets and barriers to entry are low; resist framing it as merely a social club activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Innovation and progression are needed—don't merely recreate past forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Improvisation has been surprisingly stationary; practitioners should build on Johnstone and Close intelligently and not simply re-create the same early formats without progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experiment thoughtfully, share methods, and pursue developments that advance the art rather than changing things for the sake of novelty or clinging to purity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not create outlandish games without purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid creating outlandish new games with no point or changing things for the sake of change; instead ask what you love about improvisation and explore those qualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Innovate with intent: new formats or games should teach or reveal something about performance, not just be novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality control: train performers and prevent social‑club dynamics
rubrics_metrics.description: There is little quality control in improv; groups functioning as social clubs or with poorly trained players drive innovators away.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invest in training, standards and critique within companies; make improv a place to develop great spontaneous comedy rather than a casual pastime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be transparent about improvisation when presenting shows
rubrics_metrics.description: Companies rarely would advertise or present a show without acknowledging its improvised nature because that would expose weaknesses; being open sets audience expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tell audiences up front that a show is improvised so expectations are calibrated and the work's risks are part of the entertainment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical practice (classes/workshops) outweighs passive reading for learners
rubrics_metrics.description: If you want to learn to improvise, go and take some improv classes—working with others without a script teaches more than passively reading a book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this book as a complement to hands-on classes; enrol in workshops and perform frequently to internalize skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching: emphasise craft and process over collection of gimmick games
rubrics_metrics.description: The authors focus on craft and process rather than a wide variety of 'hoop' games; teachers should prefer exercises that teach the business of improvising for performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adapt exercises into a syllabus tailored to students' needs, favouring depth (what games teach about performance) over breadth of novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Syllabus design and staged practice for new companies
rubrics_metrics.description: Exercises begin at the beginning with no prior knowledge assumed so a designated director could work through chapters to coach a new company; however, groups will often benefit from a more experienced coach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the book's progressive exercises to build a company curriculum, stage material regularly, and seek outside coaching to provide dispassionate feedback when possible.
